question: What is the main goal of a community-centred food supply system?

options.B: International cargo shipping and bulk trade
options.C: Relying entirely on imported food items
options.D: Industrial food processing and long storage

explanation: Spot on! Community-centred systems are all about linking local farmers directly with nearby folks to build strong, self-reliant regions. You've got this! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h1)

question: How does a local food network protect your neighborhood during a transport strike?

options.A: By increasing the cost of basic food items
options.B: By providing a protective buffer of nearby food sources
options.C: By shutting down local markets immediately
options.D: By depending completely on imported supplies

explanation: Exactly! When long-distance transport is blocked, having food grown right in your backyard or nearby keeps everyone fed. Great thinking! [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h1)

question: What is the main job of smallholder farmers in local food systems?

options.A: Producing only a single crop across thousands of acres
options.C: Managing international shipping ports for agricultural export
options.D: Cultivating modest plots to produce various crops for nearby markets

explanation: Well done! Smallholder farmers work smaller pieces of land to grow a nice variety of foods specifically for people living around them. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h2)

question: Why do many community farming systems encourage seed saving?

options.A: To ensure that all seeds are patented by international corporations
options.B: To preserve climate-resilient seed varieties instead of buying commercial hybrids
options.C: To increase the overall cost of planting basic vegetables
options.D: To prevent any crops from growing during the dry season

explanation: You got it! Saving seeds helps farmers keep traditional, hardy crops growing locally without always having to buy expensive commercial seeds. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h2)

question: In public health, what do we mean by 'nutritional deserts' in cities?

options.A: Dry geographic regions where no plants can ever grow
options.B: Neighborhoods that have an excess of community gardens
options.C: Industrial zones dedicated exclusively to meat processing
options.D: Areas with limited access to fresh, affordable, and healthy food

explanation: Correct! Nutritional deserts are urban spots where residents find it really hard to grab fresh, healthy food nearby. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h3)

question: A community health nurse sees poor nutrition in a crowded neighborhood with many empty lots. What is a practical step to take?

options.A: Setting up community gardens and urban farming projects on the vacant lots
options.B: Building a large international shipping port in the city center
options.C: Replacing all local food markets with fast-food outlets
options.D: Encouraging residents to travel out of state for grocery shopping

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Turning empty lots into gardens is a brilliant way to fight nutritional deserts and bring fresh food to the community. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h3)

question: What does the term 'hidden hunger' mean in public health?

options.A: Micronutrient deficiencies from diets lacking essential vitamins and minerals
options.B: Eating too many high-protein foods in a single meal
options.C: Extreme starvation caused by total crop failure
options.D: A condition where people hide their food out of fear of theft

explanation: Exactly right! Hidden hunger happens when someone gets enough belly-filling calories from cheap starchy foods, but misses out on vital vitamins and minerals. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h4)

question: Why is giving people only cheap, starchy food not enough for long-term health?

options.A: It cannot be stored in community kitchens
options.B: It causes immediate starvation within a few hours
options.C: It is always more expensive than fresh vegetables
options.D: It does not prevent micronutrient deficiencies or hidden hunger

explanation: Well reasoned! While starch gives energy, true health needs a balance of vitamins, minerals, and proteins to keep deficiency diseases away. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h4)

question: What is a major plus for local farmers when they use short food supply chains?

options.A: They earn fairer wages by cutting out intermediaries
options.B: They no longer have to harvest their own vegetables
options.C: They rely on international shipping companies to sell crops
options.D: They are forced to sell their products at a massive loss

explanation: Spot on! By removing middlemen and brokers, farmers get to keep a much fairer share of the profit from their sweat and hard work. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h5)

question: How do farmers' markets help build trust between buyers and their food?

options.A: By ensuring that all food items are processed in distant factories
options.B: By hiding the origin of the produce to protect trade secrets
options.C: By shipping all unsold food to foreign countries
options.D: By allowing buyers to ask growers directly about farming methods

explanation: Correct! Chatting face-to-face with the person who grew your food creates amazing transparency and peace of mind. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h5)

question: Besides basic nutrition science, what strongly shapes what people eat every day?

options.C: Cultural heritage, religious traditions, and socioeconomic status
options.D: Global shipping schedules and fuel prices

explanation: You got it! What we put on our plates is deeply tied to our culture, traditions, pocket, and generational habits. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h6)

question: Why do community nutrition programs sometimes struggle when they introduce unfamiliar foreign foods?

options.A: Local kitchens are physically unable to cook imported ingredients
options.B: Foreign foods contain no vitamins or minerals whatsoever
options.C: Food is deeply connected to personal identity, comfort, and tradition
options.D: Community members refuse to eat anything that has been grown locally

explanation: Spot on! Food is personal and tied to our comfort and identity. If you ignore local food culture, people naturally won't vibe with it. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h6)

question: What is a main reason fresh fruits spoil so fast after harvest in hot climates?

options.A: Excessive consumption of vegetables by local farmers
options.B: Inadequate cold storage and refrigeration facilities
options.C: Overly strict international export quality standards
options.D: The use of organic seeds instead of commercial hybrids

explanation: Correct! Without good refrigeration in hot weather, fresh produce unfortunately goes bad before it ever gets to market. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h7)

question: How do bad rural roads negatively affect a community's food security?

options.A: They cause local farmers to grow too many surplus vegetables
options.B: They make it too easy for international corporations to import food
options.C: They isolate small farms and prevent crops from reaching urban markets
options.D: They eliminate the need for community gardens and urban farms

explanation: Well done! Bad roads trap food in the villages where it might spoil, stopping it from feeding hungry city populations. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h7)

question: What is a key action public health nurses take to improve community nutrition?

options.A: Growing all the crops needed for the entire country inside hospitals
options.B: Organizing nutritional screenings and educating families on budget-friendly local meals
options.C: Passing strict laws to ban all processed foods globally
options.D: Taking over the management of international cargo shipping lines

explanation: Spot on! Nurses play a huge role by checking nutritional status and teaching families how to cook healthy, pocket-friendly local meals. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h8)

question: A nurse treats a high blood pressure patient living in a neighborhood with poor food access. What is the best all-round approach?

options.A: Provide medication while also connecting the patient to local nutritional resources and food programs
options.B: Focus solely on writing prescriptions without discussing the patient's diet
options.C: Tell the patient to only purchase expensive imported foods from distant supermarkets
options.D: Advise the patient to stop eating entirely until their blood pressure normalizes

explanation: Brilliant nursing care! Good treatment means handing out medicine while also helping the patient find practical food support right in their community. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T030#GNS227_U2_T030_h8)
